transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-05-10
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE); Diego Morales (Redwood SE); Olivia Hart (Cypress Maritime, Head of Platform); Marcus King (Cypress, ML Eng); Priya Desai (Cypress, Security); Tom Nguyen (Cypress, Procurement)

Summary:
Quick optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for a customer-facing chat agent used onboard ships. Primary goals: reduce per-token cost while keeping 95th/99th latency SLOs under 300ms and 800ms respectively for short queries; discuss hosted vs private deployment constraints (VPC + KMS), and plan a bench run with sample QPS and session traces.

Topics:
- Console walkthrough: Optimize tab (cost simulator, model profiles)
- Batching strategies and dynamic vs fixed batch sizing
- Prefix cache vs session KV cache tradeoffs
- Cost model forecasting with Cypress's traffic mix
- Security/Private deployment concerns (KMS, SOC2, audit logs)

Action items (captured at top as well): see metadata

Transcript:
00:00 Samantha: Okay, good afternoon everyone — thanks for joining. I'm Samantha Lee from Redwood. Diego and I will run through an Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and caching recommendations. We have about 50 minutes, I think, so we'll leave time for Qs.
00:13 Olivia: Hi Sam, thanks. We have a bunch of ops people on the call but I'm the platform owner. Quick context — we're running an on-prem inference stack today, a mix of A100 and some older V100s, wanting to move to a hybrid model. Primary ask is cost predictability plus complying with our maritime regs for data at rest.
00:30 Diego: Hey all. Quick intro — I'm Diego, SE on inference optimizations. We'll show the console econ-simulator, then dive into KV and prefix cache options and run a few cost scenarios.
00:45 Marcus: Hi. Our workload is a passenger chat agent — lots of short prompts (slot filling) and occasional long context (incident reports). Typical QPS is around 130 steady, spikes to 700 during check-in windows. Latency targets: p95 under 300ms, p99 under 800ms.
01:05 Priya: Hi — from security, we need encryption with customer-managed keys (KMS), audit logs for 1 year, and SSO with SAML. Also concerned about data residency when using hosted API.
01:22 Samantha: Noted. Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and audit retention options; we'll share SOC2 docs. For the econ part — Diego, show the simulator?
01:31 Diego: Sure. (background click) Alright, on my screen: the Optimize console — top-left is cost-simulator. We imported a mock traffic profile that Olivia shared earlier. Quick note: the simulator approximates token-level costs given concurrency, batching, and hit-rate assumptions for prefix/K V (sometimes transcribed as K V) cache.
01:56 Samantha: small side note — in the console we sometimes call it prefix cache and session cache; customers call it KV or K-V cache, so you'll see both names in the UI and docs.
02:07 Diego: Right. First baseline: no cache, fixed small batch size (batch=4), model is open-7b-quant, 8k context, average prompt length 40 tokens, response 60 tokens. At 130 QPS steady our simulated monthly cost is $X (placeholder in demo) — key is the relative delta when we enable prefetch or KV.
02:29 Marcus: can you show the effect of batching with higher concurrency? our bursts to 700 are short, like 10-15 minutes.
02:36 Diego: Yep. I'll toggle concurrency to 700 spike pattern — simulator recomputes. Two things happen: batching efficiency improves during spikes (amortizes kernel launch), but tail latency can increase if batch windows get too big. We model an adaptive batcher: target latency budget (p95 300ms), and it adjusts the batch cap to keep within budget.
03:05 Samantha: The key knob is the tradeoff: larger max-batch improves throughput and lowers per-token cost but risks hitting your latency SLO during low-load when the queue waiting time becomes material.
03:20 Marcus: So how does prefix cache fit? We have a lot of repeated intents — boarding status, itinerary lookups — should be high hit-rate.
03:28 Diego: Prefix cache caches KV pairs for common prompt prefixes (like system + user small context) so many short queries hit the cache and never run the full transformer. In the console I can flip cache policies — prefetch vs on-demand session cache. Prefetch warms entries based on historical frequency; session cache keeps per-session KV to accelerate multi-turn conversations.
03:48 Olivia: Which is better for us? prefet-ch or session cache?
03:52 Diego: Depends. Prefetch is great when you have high re-use across users — like static FAQs. Session cache helps with multi-turn where the user maintains context across messages. For your chat agent, probably mixed: prefetch for common intents, session cache for short dialogues.
04:10 Priya: Security question — if we use prefetch, where's the data stored? On your managed service or in our VPC?
04:18 Samantha: For Redwood Private and Dedicated, the cache lives in the customer-controlled environment. For hosted API we provide configurable retention and encryption, but data residency may not meet maritime regs — that's where Private comes in.
04:31 Tom: procurement question — what's the pricing delta between hosted and dedicated? We need ballpark to include in internal business case.
04:39 Samantha: We'll send a customized cost-model spreadsheet. Roughly, dedicated reserved capacity gives better per-token economics on steady QPS but requires commit. Hosted is flexible but higher per-token price. The simulator shows those deltas when you flip the routing policy to dedicated vs hosted.
04:55 Diego: Back to econ: here's a chart — with prefetch at 40% hit-rate, cost drops by ~37% in the model; with session cache at 25% effective hit-rate, another ~12% reduction. Combined you see compounding effects but note diminishing returns as hit-rate approaches 70-80%.
05:20 Marcus: The 40% prefetch hit-rate — realistic for us?
05:24 Diego: For FAQ-ish queries yes; but depends on prompt normalization. We recommend canonicalizing prompts server-side to increase hit-rate — e.g., strip stopwords, map synonyms — I'll include a small normalization recipe.
05:40 Samantha: Also note: KV cache effectiveness is sensitive to model changes and tokenization mismatch — if you swap model variants, cache key semantics can shift. We recommend model pinning for cache-sensitive workloads.
06:02 Olivia: Can you explain prefetch refresh policy? we worry about stale answers for schedule data.
06:10 Diego: Prefetch can use TTLs and invalidation hooks. For schedule data I'd set a short TTL (e.g., 5m) plus on-update invalidation from your downstream systems. Prefetch can be prioritized for static items and lower TTL for frequently-changing entries.
06:29 Priya: audit log question again — do you log cache hits as part of request lineage?
06:36 Samantha: Yes, audit logs include whether result returned from cache vs full model, and include keys (redacted) and timestamps. We can increase retention to a year on Private.
06:49 Marcus: re batching — what's the recommended target batch size for our model and context lengths?
06:55 Diego: For open-7b-quant and your average lengths, a dynamic cap of 8-16 is a good start. The console sim shows diminishing returns beyond 16 because of memory layout and KV lookup costs; but if you move to larger models or longer contexts, that changes.
07:16 Marcus: how do we handle concurrent sessions? do we need session affinity?
07:20 Diego: Session affinity helps with hot KV cache locality — if a user can be routed to the same runtime, session cache hit-rate increases. For Dedicated you can enable session-affinity policies; for Hosted we have sticky routing options per-tenant.
07:37 Olivia: We have a multi-region requirement, ships travel — do you support geo-routing for low latency and legal constraints?
07:45 Samantha: Yes, smart routing can route by region and fallback to another region; we also do auto-fallback to a smaller model if the primary region doesn't have capacity. For compliance we can pin processing to specific regions under Private.
08:00 Tom: If we go Private, how long to deploy? We're on a tight procurement cycle.
08:06 Samantha: Typical Private deployments take 4-8 weeks depending on networking and approvals; Dedicated can be faster (~2 weeks) if it's cloud-hosted. We'll include an onboarding timeline in the follow-up.
08:22 Diego: Now I'll run a small 'what-if' scenario — toggling prefetch hit-rate from 0% to 60% and adjusting batch caps.
08:30 (console clicks) 08:33 Diego: At 0% prefetch baseline, monthly cost for your profile is Y. At 20% prefetch, cost drops ~18%. At 40% it's ~36% less. At 60% we hit 50% reduction but see slight p99 latency decrease because cache bypasses model entirely.
08:55 Marcus: Is the simulator using real kernel-level efficiencies or is it an estimate?
08:59 Diego: It's an estimate calibrated to our runtime benchmarks — kernel selection, batching overhead, KV lookup times are profiled; but we'll run a bench with your exact payload to validate. That's why Diego suggested a 4-hour bench.
09:12 Olivia: You mentioned prefetch warming from historical data — do you need all our logs to do that?
09:19 Diego: Ideally we'd get anonymized traces showing frequently occurring prefixes. We can also provide a tool to generate a candidate prefetch list from your logs without sending raw PII.
09:28 Priya: That would help. For compliance we prefer an on-prem tool to compute candidate lists and push them to our private cache.
09:34 Samantha: We can support both — we have an offline prefetch generator you can run inside your VPC to produce the seed list.
09:42 Marcus: A question on quantization and cache: if we quantize further for throughput, does cache still behave the same?
09:48 Diego: Cache keys are model-agnostic if you keep tokenization consistent. But model changes that affect tokenization (different tokenizer or BPE merges) will change keys. So pin the model and quant config for cache validity.
10:05 Olivia: Any gotchas with prefetch and personalized content? We can't accidentally serve another passenger's itinerary.
10:13 Diego: Very important — prefetch is for non-personal, static items. Personal data must be session-scoped and mustn't be shared. We support strict key scoping and redaction to prevent cross-session leakage.
10:26 Priya: KMS detail — do you integrate with our on-prem HSM?
10:31 Samantha: Yes, via standard KMIP/HSM integrations on Private. We'll include the connector docs.
10:38 Tom: Commercial question — will the bench be included in pilot or cost extra?
10:44 Samantha: We typically include a pilot bench as part of evaluation for strategic deals; we'll flag this in the follow-up and include recommended scope for the bench.
10:55 Diego: Quick demo of our 'savings forecast' CSV export — it shows cost per 1M tokens under each policy and the expected delta. I'll export and share after the call.
11:08 Marcus: Are there visualizations for tail latency distribution when batching increases?
11:12 Diego: Yes — console chart shows latency percentiles across load patterns. You can overlay cost vs p95/p99 to pick an operating point.
11:22 Olivia: Ok, procurement timeline — we need the pricing and SOC2 before legal signs off. Tom will need a ballpark by EOD Monday.
11:31 Tom: yes
11:33 Samantha: We'll aim to get the price ballpark + SOC2 link by Monday EOD. Action items: Sam share docs; Diego run bench; Marcus send traces.
11:43 (brief crosstalk)
11:50 Speaker 1 (transcription quirk): uh so like the prefetch, if — if you can automate the key gen — that would save ops, right
11:58 Diego: yes, we provide a helper script to generate keys and TTLs from historical frequency.
12:06 Marcus: one last question — can we do partial rollout? like prefetch only for top 10 intents then gradually increase?
12:12 Samantha: Absolutely — the console supports canarying prefetch policies, and you can rollback or set TTLs to zero for problematic keys.
12:21 Priya: Also we'd need to ensure audit events are forwarded to our SIEM — is that supported?
12:27 Samantha: Yes, SIEM forwarding and syslog/JSON endpoints are supported; we'll include config examples.
12:34 Olivia: Great, thanks. That's very actionable.
12:37 Samantha: OK let's recap.
12:40 Samantha (recap): 1) Redwood to send cost-model spreadsheet, SOC2 + architecture + KMS connector docs by 2028-05-11. 2) Diego to run bench with Cypress payload (4 hours) and share metrics by 2028-05-16. 3) Marcus to send sample traces and QPS profile by 2028-05-15. 4) Schedule follow-up week of 2028-05-22 to review bench and procurement.
13:05 Olivia: Works for us. Thanks everyone.
13:09 Samantha: Thanks, we'll follow up. Bye.
13:12 (call ends)

Notes about transcription quality: occasional speaker mislabels and 'K V' spacing. Some numbers (cost placeholders) intentionally omitted in the demo recording; spreadsheet will have precise values.
